_source: Mushrooms of the Pacific Northwest (2009) [9780881929355], ch02.html (Light-Spored Gilled Mushrooms), ch04.html (Brown-Spored Gilled Mushrooms), ch06.html (Boletes), ch07.html (Spine-Fungi), ch08.html (Club-, Coral-, and Fan-like Fungi), ch09.html (Polypores and Crust-Fungi), ch10.html (Puffballs, Earthballs, and Earthstars), ch11.html (Jelly-like Fungi), ch12.html (Morels, False Morels, and Elfin Saddles), ch13.html (Cup-Fungi), app01.html (Appendix 1: Types of Mushroom Poisoning)
_note: Vocabulary-coverage pass. Species were chosen to span fruit-body forms, not for dataset completeness. See accompanying report for pooled new-vocabulary and unmapped-characteristic findings and the stated-vs-form-implied absence ratio.

species.habitat: Forests and urban plantings with birch, spruce, and pine; a paler orange-capped form is common with planted birches and under spruce and pine

_evidence.cap: "the color of the cap, which ranges from white to yellows and oranges, to deep red and even brown"; "All the forms have striate cap margins"; white 'polka dots' = universal veil warts
_evidence.stipe: "volvas in the form of rings of loose tissue that extend part way up the stipe from a bulbous base"; "rings that may or may not persist into maturity"
_evidence.trees: "a paler form common with planted birches and under spruce and pine" (stated for one colour form, not the whole species — flagged low confidence)
_evidence.edibility: "Along with Amanita gemmata, A. pantherina, and A. aprica, all contain ibotenic acid. Thus, they cause accidental poisonings" (ch02); ibotenic acid confirmed as the causative toxin in Appendix 1
_evidence.nutrition: genus-level: "Nearly all the PNW species appear to be ectomycorrhizal" (not muscaria-specific)

_newVocabulary.note: universal-veil remnants left as raised bumps on the cap — a core Amanita diagnostic word, distinct from 'scaly'

_unmapped.value: red/yellowish-veil, orange/white-veil, and white/white-veil forms all illustrated for this one species
_unmapped.verdict: out of scope for a single tag set; the record can only show what's typical, not the whole documented range — noted here so a reviewer knows the tags undersell the variability

species.lookalikes: Tricholoma flavovirens (per the guide's genus-level confusion note); Amanita ocreata, a similar all-white relative also deadly
species.habitat: Introduced and naturalized with oak and in hazel (filbert) orchards; expected to spread into natural PNW forests

_evidence.cap: "usually has an olive to greenish yellow or yellowish brown to bronze cap, often with darker streaks, but not striations, on the margin; occasionally it occurs in a white form"
_evidence.hymenium: "white gills that may be slightly attached or free" (destroying-angel group description, applies directly to this species)
_evidence.stipe: "a membranous outer veil that leaves a sac-like volva on the enlarged stipe base... and a partial veil that typically forms a ring"
_evidence.sporePrint: "All have white amyloid spores" (destroying-angel group, three species including this one)
_evidence.trees: "In urban areas, A. phalloides occurs with a variety of trees including oak; it also is found in hazel (filbert) orchards"
_evidence.edibility: "Amanita phalloides and its relative A. ocreata... both members of the destroying angel group, definitely occur in the PNW... All these species can cause deadly poisoning"; amatoxins confirmed in Appendix 1

_newVocabulary.note: negative form of 'striate' — a stated diagnostic (this group's margin explicitly lacks striations, unlike A. muscaria's), and 'striate' with no way to say 'definitely not' is a real gap
a metallic cap tone distinct from the existing browns/olives
darker radial streaks over a paler ground colour — different from 'zonate' (concentric bands) or 'fibrillose'

_unmapped.verdict: chemical/microscopy test (Melzer's reagent), out of scope for the tag set — but genuinely diagnostic for the destroying-angel group

species.lookalikes: Psilocybe stuntzii (deadly mistake documented in the region); honey mushroom, Armillaria spp. (distinguished by brown, not white, spores)
species.habitat: Stumps and logs of conifers and hardwoods, or from buried wood, wood chips, and other woody debris

_evidence.cap: "a dome-shaped, brown to yellow-brown cap that is smooth, slightly viscid to moist, striate along the edge when fresh, and fades to tan or buff"
_evidence.stipe: "the veil sometimes leaves a fibrillose ring-zone on the stipe"
_evidence.sporePrint: "All galerinas have rich brown to rust-brown spores" (genus intro, directly preceding this species)
_evidence.edibility: "By any name it is just as deadly, containing the same toxins found in Amanita phalloides... at least one death and several close calls have occurred in our region"
_evidence.lookalikes: "mistaking it for a psychoactive species such as Psilocybe stuntzii... could also be mistaken for a honey mushroom, although it is usually much smaller and has brown, not white, spores"

_newVocabulary.note: a partial/fading marking left by the veil, distinct from a true persistent 'ring' — recurs across several genera in this guide (also Suillus, below) and deserves its own vocabulary entry rather than being folded into 'ring'
the guide's own word for a rounded, not-quite-convex cap profile; close to but not identical to 'convex'

species.lookalikes: Hygrophoropsis aurantiaca; Chroogomphus tomentosus; Omphalotus olivascens (California, poisonous)
species.habitat: Soil, or sometimes well-rotted wood, in moist PNW woodland

_evidence.cap: "a dull orange to brownish orange cap that readily bruises brownish and often is finely scaly"
_evidence.hymenium: "the fertile ridges often are deep and relatively thin; they are usually pale orange-yellow but may have a pinkish cast"; genus-wide, chanterelles "bear their spores on ridges instead of plate-like gills"
_evidence.edibility: "C. formosus fruits abundantly... and is the species most commonly found for sale in produce markets and grocery stores, as well as on restaurant menus"; sibling species are elsewhere called "good edibles"
_evidence.lookalikes: "Gilled mushrooms that could be confused with golden chanterelles include Hygrophoropsis aurantiaca, Chroogomphus tomentosus, and, in California, Omphalotus olivascens"

_newVocabulary.note: stipe build word, distinct from 'tapering' (shape) — commonly paired with it in the source

_unmapped.value: "good edibles" / commercial-market prominence, without the words 'choice' or 'prized'
_unmapped.verdict: a real scale-mapping tension: the guide's habitual phrase for chanterelles is milder than its language for morels ("highly sought-after"), yet real-world market demand argues for 'choice'. Mapped choice here on the strength of the market/restaurant sentence, but flagged as a judgment call worth a second look.

species.habitat: Mossy, rotten wood; long fruiting season, uncommon in winter in most of the PNW

_evidence.cap: "a small, slender, trumpet-shaped chanterelle with a brownish or orange-brown cap"
_evidence.substrate: "penchant for growing on mossy rotten wood"
_evidence.edibility: "Despite its size, C. tubaeformis is edible and considered choice by some" (hedged — mapped to the more cautious 'edible')

_newVocabulary.note: the guide's own recurring word for this group ("vase-, funnel-, or trumpet-shaped"); close to but not the same shape word as 'infundibuliform'

_unmapped.value: not separately described — only the genus-wide 'spores on ridges' statement is available
_unmapped.verdict: left unrecorded rather than assumed; noted because it shows how much a species entry can lean on its genus intro before there's nothing left to attribute to the species itself

species.lookalikes: Boletus fibrillosus (edible, but inferior to B. edulis)
species.habitat: Conifer forest, old-growth and earlier-succession stands

_evidence.cap: "the cap surface is moist to viscid... color... ranges from almost whitish to various shades of brown to reddish brown"
_evidence.hymenium: "firm whitish tubes and pores... that become yellow to olive and soft-gelatinous with age"
_evidence.stipe: "The stipe is reticulate at least at the apex, typically fleshy and club-shaped, whitish at the apex and some shade of brown below"
_evidence.sporePrint: genus-level: "[spore color] ranges from brown to olive-brown in Boletus and Leccinum" (not edulis-specific)
_evidence.edibility: "Boletus edulis and its close relatives are commonly collected for food and known variously as porcini, ceps, steinpilz, and king boletes" — mapped to the more cautious 'edible' rather than 'choice' since the guide never uses that word for it

_unmapped.value: "a bolete left sitting out at room temperature overnight or longer will turn into an odorous mass of mush"
_unmapped.verdict: a genuinely diagnostic bolete-group trait (separates true boletes from look-alike polypores) with nowhere to go in the current character set — worth a descriptor tag ('putrescent') if boletes become a large share of the library

species.habitat: Under Douglas-fir, often fruiting with Suillus caerulescens and gomphidiuses

_evidence.cap: "a reddish to red-brown or orange-buff, dry to viscid, fibrillose-scaly cap"
_evidence.stipe: "a veil that leaves a distinct ring-zone, and a stipe that is yellowish above"
_evidence.sporePrint: genus-level: "olive-brown to vinaceous brown in Suillus" (not lakei-specific)
_evidence.staining: "typically stain reddish brown when bruised"; "The flesh of the stipe base sometimes turns bluish when exposed"
_evidence.edibility: genus-level: "Most suilluses are edible, but few of them make many top-ten lists" (not lakei-specific)

_newVocabulary.note: a wine-tinted brown, standard mycological colour term, distinct from 'brown' or 'red-brown'

species._lowConfidenceReason: Edibility and spore colour are both genus-level statements, not species-specific; the species paragraph itself gives good cap/stipe/staining detail but the guide never circles back to name Suillus lakei's own edibility or spore-print colour directly.

species.habitat: Conifer forest, ectomycorrhizal on nutrient-poor soils (chapter-level)

_evidence.cap: "distinguished by their pale cream to creamy orangish coloration... and soft texture of the flesh"
_evidence.hymenium: "soft icicle-like spines on the caps" — recorded rather than marked absent; see _form note below
_evidence.substrate: chapter-level: "these fungi are ectomycorrhizal, especially with conifers on sandy or otherwise nutrient-poor soils" (not repandum-specific)
_evidence.edibility: "All are very popular edibles" (mapped to the more cautious 'edible' rather than 'choice')

_newVocabulary.note: the guide's own shape word for hanging spines, distinct from a plain 'teeth' tag

species._formTableOverride: The task's form table marks hydnoid's 'Gills/pores' cell as ABSENT ('teeth, neither'). But model.js's own FUNGI_CHARACTERS vocab for the 'hymenium' character explicitly lists 'teeth' as a suggested tag — meaning the schema's designer clearly intended tooth-fungi to be RECORDED under hymenium (tag: teeth), not marked na. Followed the schema's actual vocabulary here rather than the table; flagged as a form-table/schema mismatch for the vocabulary curator to resolve — either the table's wording needs softening for hydnoid, or 'teeth' should be pulled from the hymenium vocab and given its own character.

species.habitat: Conifer logs, especially fir and hemlock

_evidence.hymenium: "The branches and spines are whitish when young, and become yellowish in age"
_evidence.substrate: "It grows on conifer logs, especially those of fir and hemlock"
_evidence.edibility: "All are edible, good, and eagerly sought by mycophagists" — "eagerly sought" read as equivalent to 'prized', mapped to choice
_evidence.nutrition: Species-specific substrate (conifer logs) points to a wood-decay habit; this conflicts with the chapter's own generalization (see _unmapped) that spine-fungi other than Auriscalpium are ectomycorrhizal — the species-specific evidence was preferred over the chapter generalization.

_unmapped.value: a branched, cap-less coral bearing spines directly on its branches — not a capped, spine-bearing structure like Hydnum
_unmapped.verdict: Hericium doesn't cleanly fit either the hydnoid or clavarioid row of the form table (branched like a coral, toothed like a hydnoid). Left cap and stipe unrecorded rather than force an na claim the table doesn't actually support for this species — worth its own hybrid row or a note that 'hydnoid' covers two distinct architectures.

species._disagreement: The chapter intro states 'With the exception of Auriscalpium, these fungi are ectomycorrhizal' for the spine-fungi group, which by its placement would seem to include Hericium — but Hericium abietis's own paragraph describes it strictly as a wood-log fungus, the classic saprophyte pattern. Nutrition was set to saprophytic on the species-specific evidence; flagging the tension for review rather than silently picking a side.

species.lookalikes: Ramaria magnipes (brighter coloured, slightly longer spores)
species.habitat: Soil, often buried and covered in litter; a common member of the PNW spring mycota

_evidence.stipe: "The stipe does not bruise brown and does not react with iron sulfate, but does exhibit a very slow, weak amyloid reaction." — recorded as present (bare tag, no further descriptive detail available) because the clavarioid default ('the club is the body') is directly contradicted by the text naming a distinct stipe
_evidence.sporePrint: genus-level: "the spores are cream to yellowish, ocher, or pale brownish" (Ramaria genus intro, not rasilispora-specific)
_evidence.trees: genus-level: "many of the PNW species [of Ramaria and Laeticolora] seem particularly fond of hemlock" (not rasilispora-specific)
_evidence.edibility: "All these are eaten by many people" — laxative effects noted "in some people" for related varieties, kept at 'edible' rather than escalated to 'toxic' since the guide itself calls it an edible species and the effect is mild and inconsistent, not gastric illness

_unmapped.value: "does not react with iron sulfate"; "a very slow, weak amyloid reaction"
_unmapped.verdict: standard coral-fungus id tests (iron sulfate, Melzer's/amyloid) — worth a dedicated chemical-test field if corals or boletes become a large share of the library

_unmapped.value: printed in the source as "8–115 × 3–45 µm" — almost certainly "8–11.5 × 3–4.5 µm" with decimal points lost in typesetting
_unmapped.verdict: a data-quality flag rather than a schema gap; noted so nobody copies the malformed figure forward

_unmapped.value: "Orson Miller reported that, in some people, it has laxative effects"
_unmapped.verdict: the edibility scale has no rung between 'edible' and 'toxic' for a mild, inconsistent GI effect — a real gap for the coral-fungi genus as a whole

species.habitat: With conifers, throughout the Northern Hemisphere

_evidence.cap: "produces rather large fruit-bodies with a wide flattened cap, which makes it look something like a chanterelle" — recorded rather than marked absent because this species explicitly overrides the clavarioid default; colour from genus intro ("characteristic ocher to yellow-orange color")
_evidence.hymenium: "the fertile surface, which runs down the upper portion beneath the 'cap,' is wrinkled" — recorded rather than marked absent, for the same reason
_evidence.scent: "Clavariadelphus truncatus is edible, with a rather sweet taste"
_evidence.edibility: "Clavariadelphus truncatus is edible, with a rather sweet taste"

species._formTableOverride: The clavarioid row of the form table marks cap and hymenium absent by default ('a smooth surface'). This species is the table's own stated exception: the guide explicitly compares its wide flattened top and wrinkled fertile surface to a chanterelle's cap and ridges. Recorded both rather than defaulting to na — a clean example of the table being defeated by its own source text.

species.lookalikes: Heterobasidion annosum (similar when growing shelf-like, but lacks reddish colors)
species.habitat: Brown-rot on conifers, occasionally hardwoods (especially black cherry)

_evidence.cap: "The surface of the cap is usually banded with orange, reddish orange, or grayish to black, and has a whitish rounded edge"
_evidence.hymenium: "The pores are very small and white, yellowish when bruised"
_evidence.staining: "pores are very small and white, yellowish when bruised"
_evidence.trees: "Fomitopsis pinicola causes a brown-rot primarily in conifers, but occasionally in hardwoods, especially black cherry"

_newVocabulary.note: flesh texture word specific to hard perennial polypores; surprising gap given how central it is to identifying conks

_unmapped.value: "causes a brown-rot" vs. white-rot (stated for Ganoderma, Heterobasidion, elsewhere in the same chapter)
_unmapped.verdict: ecologically important for polypores and used constantly by the guide to distinguish genera — worth a dedicated field if polypores become a large share of the library, otherwise skip

species.lookalikes: Trametes ochracea; Stereum spp. (similar but with a smooth undersurface, no pores)

_evidence.cap: "The velvety to silky caps with concentric zones of different colors—white, buff, yellowish, brown, reddish brown, blue, and black"
_evidence.hymenium: "The pores are white to yellowish white or grayish"
_evidence.trees: "occurring extensively on hard-wood substrates and rarely on conifer wood"

_newVocabulary.note: surface texture between 'velvety' and 'smooth', paired with velvety in the source's own description

_unmapped.value: "has a history of medicinal use in Asian cultures and now is the subject of western medical research"

species.lookalikes: Morganella pyriformis (sterile base stays white at maturity); Vascellum pratense (papery membrane above the sterile base)
species.habitat: Disturbed sites — forest roadsides, campgrounds, trailhead parking areas

_evidence.stipe: genus-level: "Some puffballs—such as those in the genera Lycoperdon and Vascellum—have a sterile base that functions like a stipe and elevates the spore sac into the air" — recorded rather than marked absent on this direct statement
_evidence.sporePrint: "the olive-brown spores are propelled by a bellows action when the spore sac is hit by raindrops" — recorded despite the gasteroid default of 'no print obtainable', because the spore-mass colour itself is stated even though a traditional print can't be taken
_evidence.substrate: "can be found in disturbed sites, such as forest roadsides, from late summer through fall"

_newVocabulary.note: roadsides, campgrounds, and trail edges are a recurring niche for ruderal fungi (also Aleuria aurantia, below) with no equivalent in the current habitat vocabulary, which is built entirely around trees and wood

_unmapped.characteristic: overall/gross colour with no cap or hymenium to hang it on
_unmapped.value: "typically are white at first and become brownish in age"
_unmapped.verdict: the single biggest recurring gap in this whole pass — see the main report

_evidence.stipe: "Its spore case sits directly on the usually five- to eight-rayed base formed by the thick outer peridium, unlike many species in which the spore case is elevated on a short stipe" — an explicit, species-specific statement, not a form assumption
_evidence.trees: "One small to medium-sized species that is found in PNW conifer forests is Geastrum saccatum"

species.habitat: Hardwood wood, often where the crust fungus Stereum hirsutum is also fruiting

_evidence.trees: "Tremella mesenterica is similar in appearance and texture, but grows on hardwoods and often is associated with the wood-rotting fungus Stereum hirsutum"

_unmapped.value: "often is associated with the wood-rotting fungus Stereum hirsutum"
_unmapped.verdict: the nutrition enum (saprophytic/mycorrhizal/both) has no slot for a species parasitic on another fungus rather than on wood or a tree root directly — genuinely a different ecological mode, not a wording gap

species.lookalikes: Verpa bohemica and Gyromitra esculenta (false morels) — Verpa's cap hangs free except at the very apex; Gyromitra's cap is brain-like and wrinkled rather than honeycombed with pits, and is often partly fused to the stipe

_evidence.substrate: "occurs in spring to early summer with conifers and hardwoods, in plantings, orchards, and burned areas"
